03e1177299f4bd3a: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 13 — The first of two days of the Pokemon PokéXciting! celebrations at KLCC Park ended with a spectacular drone show, a fittingly satisfying end to the day’s celebrations.
While the PokéXciting! scheduled events didn’t officially start until 1pm, fans arrived early yesterday to check out the Pokémon-themed decorations as well as Pokémon Go activities.
Fans were able to collect virtual stamps and medals from Pokémon Go as well as the Pokémon HOME app for Pokémon storage and trade.
There were also booths to collect yellow sun visors with Pikachu ears, which were very handy in the day’s heat.
@ernamh A preview of what’s available at Malaysia’s first ever Pokémon Pop-up store. #pokemon #pokexciting KISS N TELL - aespa
Calm, orderly
Despite the searing mid-afternoon heat, huge crowds assembled in KLCC Park to watch the mascot parade, stage show and also chase Pokémon around in the Pokémon Go mobile game.
The increased footfall for the day led to restaurants and food kiosks seeing long lines, with queues even for the escalator from the lower ground to the ground floor entrance to KLCC Park.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The Petronas Towers glowed green to match Bulbasaur, a delightful syncing along to the performance. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Despite the crowds, heat and the presence of many small humans (children will always insert a small element of chaos into any situation), KLCC and the organisers seem to have kept things orderly.
It was striking to see people so patiently queuing for giveaways such as the cute yellow Pikachu sun visors that both children and adults donned happily, even wearing them inside the mall.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Huge crowds gathered in the vicinity of the park to watch the drone show. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
There was a proportionate number of staff and security on hand to manage the very large numbers of not just Pokémon fans and locals, but tourists as well.
Dazzling lights
The biggest surprise of the show was KL Tower being an unexpected centrepiece, instead of the Petronas Towers (which took over later).
The light show properly began with KL Tower flashing a series of colourful lights to a very delighted response from the audience.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Char, char: The Petronas Towers glowed red alongside Charmander. — Picture by Raymond Manue
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Pikachu also got the Petronas Towers treatment during the light show. — Picture by Raymond Manuel

Then from that introduction, the show began proper with the nearby Petronas Twin Towers glowing in different colours and lighting designs to match each drone scene, for instance, glowing green to match the Grass Pokémon Bulbasaur.
From Pikachu to Bulbasaur, Charmander and Squirtle, the show paid tribute to the original Kanto starters and many other well-known Pokémon figures as well as their evolutions.
Credit also has to be given to the sound direction, with popular and recognisable themes playing throughout as well as Pikachu’s trademark “Pika, pika.”
While ten minutes seemed brief, it was an enjoyable enough show that would also not be too long for young children or very tired adults.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Let’s hope that the Pokémon franchise returns to Malaysia with more events. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Most heartening was the final drone scene with the simple “Jumpa lagi, KL (See you again, Kuala Lumpur)” emblazoned in the sky alongside a silhouette of Pikachu.
Here’s hoping that there will be more events involving everyone’s favourite Pocket Monsters in Malaysia and perhaps our own Pokémon Centre?

Anyway, today is the final day of the Pokémon celebrations, so head to the park to check out the statues and if you’re staying for the drone show tonight, make your way to the outdoor area near the mosque for a better view.
Also an option: watching it from Ombak KLCC, which also has a decent view of the drone show.
Don’t forget to stay hydrated and put safety first given the large crowds.
3a7ed991cc64df18: PETALING JAYA: Retaining doctors in Malaysia’s public healthcare system will be the Malaysian Medical Association’s top priority under its new president, Dr Sivanaesan Letchumanan.
MMA said Sivanaesan, a family medicine practitioner, has held various leadership roles in the association, including chairman of MMA Selangor, and chairman of its private practitioners section

Speaking at the MMA annual banquet in Ipoh yesterday, Sivanaesan said retaining doctors was crucial as Malaysia faced rising healthcare demands from an ageing population and increasing non-communicable diseases (NCDs).

He said simply increasing the number of medical graduates would not solve the problem, with greater attention needed on career progression, working conditions, professional development, and opportunities to specialise and subspecialise.
“Training a doctor takes many years and requires significant investment. When experienced doctors leave the public system, we lose their experience, expertise and continuity of care,” he said.

Sivanaesan also called for a clearer and more predictable pathway for doctors seeking specialisation and subspecialisation, saying this would support both career development and workforce planning while helping retain talent.
On private healthcare, he said MMA would continue engaging stakeholders on issues involving third-party administrators and insurers.
He also urged the government to make greater use of more than 11,000 private GPs nationwide in preventing, detecting and managing NCDs, saying they offered convenient access to patients.
Sivanaesan said the health ministry’s “One Person, One Record” digital medical records initiative, expected within months, could enable stronger public-private collaboration.
He said the increased digital health allocation, from RM650 million to RM1 billion, could accelerate implementation.
He also said Malaysia must prepare for an ageing population by strengthening chronic disease management, rehabilitation, long-term care and other support services.

Sivanaesan expressed sadness over the Sept 8 helicopter crash near the Long Lellang short take-off and landing airport in Ulu Baram, Sarawak, which killed five people, including four healthcare workers on a Flying Doctor Service mission.
He said the tragedy highlighted the risks faced by healthcare workers serving remote communities, and stressed the need for appropriate safety measures, resources and support.
0f49c87300d484ed: KUALA LUMPUR: Youth and Sports Minister Dr Taufiq Johari may have won the race against Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, but he was quick to offer his fellow cabinet colleague a chance to settle the score.
Taufiq jokingly claimed bragging rights after edging Fahmi in the final stretch of the Oxyenergy Media Prima Merdeka Run at Balai Berita here today.
The friendly rivalry added a light-hearted touch to the event, which brought together about 1,500 participants.
After finishing the run, Taufiq challenged Fahmi to a rematch at a future programme organised by the Youth and Sports Ministry.
The fun aside, Taufiq said events such as the run were important in encouraging Malaysians to lead healthier lifestyles while strengthening national unity.
"I commend programmes like this. It is a very good initiative and one of the efforts towards achieving a healthier Malaysia," said Taufiq.

"Independence celebrations also help foster the spirit of unity among people of different races, ethnicities and religions. Today, we can see Malays, Chinese, Indians and persons with disabilities all coming together and participating with us."

Taufiq said such programmes were also part of the Youth and Sports Ministry's efforts leading up to National Sports Day in October, with a focus on encouraging more people to embrace an active lifestyle.
Fahmi, the Lembah Pantai MP, said the run also gave him an opportunity to spend time with the local community while taking part in a healthy activity.
"I would like to thank Media Prima Club for organising today's run," Fahmi said.
"As the Communications Minister and also the Lembah Pantai MP, Media Prima is part of my constituency. So, naturally, I wanted to spend time with the community and take part in a healthy activity."
The run, which started and finished at Balai Berita, featured three-kilometre and five-kilometre categories, as well as a special category for persons with disabilities.
Glasgow Commonwealth Games weightlifting gold medallists Aniq Kasdan and Aznil Bidin also took part in the inaugural event.
2fca943c1eb07fec: IPOH: Before a limestone hill disappears from the Kinta Valley landscape, Ching Boon Tat makes sure he has photographed it.
For the 43-year-old mechanic, the photographs are more than images, they are evidence — a record of the valley's natural heritage that may otherwise be lost forever, unnoticed.

As the world celebrates the first International Day of Caves and Karst today, Ching hopes greater attention will be given to the caves, limestone hills and underground systems that have shaped the Kinta Valley for millions of years.

Ching, fondly known as Ah Tat, said he had spent years documenting limestone hills, caves, rivers and other geological features across the valley, driven by concern that some could eventually disappear.
"When they are gone, I still have the photographs. At least there is a record of what was there," he said.
A mechanic by profession, Ching has no formal training in geology but developed an interest in the valley through years of observing its rivers, caves and limestone formations.
His work repairing engines and dealing with corrosion taught him to pay close attention to how materials change and deteriorate over time.
That habit eventually led him to explore the Kinta Valley, where he began documenting its landscape through photographs and field notes.
He also explores parts of the Kinta River by kayak, allowing him to observe the relationship between the river, limestone formations and surrounding landscape.
Some of his photographs have captured fossils embedded in limestone, remnants of ancient marine life that existed hundreds of millions of years ago.
"When you find fossils, you realise this land was once under the sea. You begin to understand how old and valuable it is," he said.
Ching founded Kinta Valley Watch in 2018 to document the valley's limestone landscape and raise public awareness of its geological and environmental importance.
The volunteer group documents limestone formations, maps river corridors and shares information with the public.
Ching said the Kinta Valley should be viewed as one interconnected landscape rather than a collection of individual hills.
"The Kinta Valley is a system. It stretches from Sungai Siput in the north to Kampar in the south, covering Ipoh, Tambun, Jelapang and Gopeng.
"Everything is connected like the hills, water, rivers and even the food," he said.
He said limestone was a non-renewable resource and once a hill was quarried or destroyed, its caves, fossils and underground water systems could not be replaced.
Ching said the International Day of Caves and Karst was an opportunity for people to better understand what lay beneath and around the limestone landscapes they saw every day.
For him, however, documentation remains an important part of conservation.
"I don't have power and I don't have money. I document, I explain and I share. If one day people ask what was here before, I can show them the photographs," he said.
His growing collection now serves as a visual record of the Kinta Valley including places that have changed or may no longer exist.
"These hills are not just rocks. They are nature's history. Once they are gone, there is no replacement," he said.

5282c798e38e778f: KUALA LUMPUR: Foreign investors remain supportive of Malaysia's debt market, recording RM900 million of net inflows into Malaysian bonds last week, said Kenanga Research.
In contrast, the firm said foreign institutions recorded RM640.3 million in net outflows from Bursa Malaysia during the week.
"We expect yields to hold an upward bias into the September Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), then retrace as the hike premium unwinds on a Federal Reserve hold," it said in a note.
Malaysian Government Securities (MGS) and Government Investment Issues (GII) yields rose sharply across the curve last week, increasing between 11.3 and 24.5 basis points.
The 10-year MGS yield rose 21.5 basis points to 4.134 per cent, while the 10-year GII yield increased 23.1 basis points to 4.153 per cent.
Kenanga Research said the sell-off split roughly evenly between global and domestic forces.
"Rising US Treasury and UK gilt yields lifted global benchmarks, while escalating West Asia tensions drove a sharp rebound in oil prices, adding to inflation concerns.
"Domestically, the move was led by the long end of the curve, resulting in a steepening of the three-year to 10-year (3s10s) curve," it said.
Looking forward, Kenanga Research said investors will focus on labour market and retail sales data this week, followed by trade and inflation releases next week.

The firm has raised its forecasts for the 10-year MGS yield for the third quarter of 2026 and end-2026 to 3.95 per cent and 3.88 per cent respectively, from 3.70 per cent and 3.63 per cent previously.
"This is reflecting persistent upward pressure from escalating West Asia tensions and the resulting repricing in global rates," it added.
b266ef1a58466bc2: PETALING JAYA: Perdana Menteri, Anwar Ibrahim berkata terdapat negara yang enggan mengiktiraf punca tercetusnya konflik Asia Barat membabitkan Amerika Syarikat (AS), Israel dan Iran.
Tegasnya, mengutuk serangan oleh Iran tidak bercanggah usaha mengenal pasti tindakan awal yang menyebabkan konflik itu berlaku.

Dalam wawancara bersama NDTV di luar Sidang Kemuncak BRICS di New Delhi, India, beliau menggesa pertempuran dihentikan, tetapi menegaskan sebarang perbincangan ke arah itu perlu bermula dengan pengiktirafan terhadap "pencerobohan awal" oleh Washington dan Tel Aviv.
"Konflik terkini yang dikatakan membabitkan Iran berpunca daripada pencerobohan awal AS, dan sudah tentu pada mulanya dilakukan Israel.
"Banyak negara enggan menerima mengakui fakta sebenar. Fakta itu ialah hentikan pencerobohan berterusan," katanya sambil menegaskan konflik Asia Barat memerlukan penyelesaian damai.

Ditanya sama ada Iran dan AS mengambil "pendirian ekstrem" yang boleh menyukarkan penyelesaian itu, Anwar berkata: "Hentikan keganasan. Maksud saya, keganasan yang dilakukan AS, Israel atau Iran. Saya sokong langkah itu."
Anwar membincangkan pelbagai isu, termasuk perkembangan geopolitik global dengan beberapa pemimpin dunia yang menghadiri Sidang Kemuncak BRICS.

Antara pemimpin ditemuinya pada majlis makan malam malam tadi ialah Presiden Mesir Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, Presiden Indonesia Prabowo Subianto, Presiden Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev dan Timbalan Perdana Menteri Uzbekistan Jamshid Kuchkarov.
Beliau turut menemui Setiausaha Agung Pertubuhan Bangsa-bangsa Bersatu, António Guterres dan Ketua Pengarah Pertubuhan Perdagangan Dunia, Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala.
"Bicara kami menyentuh perkembangan geopolitik dunia, khususnya konflik dan krisis kemanusiaan yang terus berlarutan di Gaza serta ketegangan di Asia Barat," katanya menurut Bernama.
Beliau berkata, keadaan itu menuntut kesatuan masyarakat dan pimpinan dunia untuk menghentikan pertumpahan darah serta mengusahakan penyelesaian adil dan berkekalan.
6eac035de505551c: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 13 — Clinique is taking the longstanding online love for its pink Moisture Surge moisturiser beyond the bathroom shelf — from Reddit conversations inspiring a new global campaign to an immersive pink takeover in Kuala Lumpur.

The beauty brand recently debuted its global “Feels Like Moisture Surge” campaign starring British actress Emilia Jones, with its creative concept inspired by real consumer comments sourced from Reddit about the Moisture Surge 100H Auto-Replenishing Hydrator.
Rather than simply focusing on what the moisturiser does, the campaign draws on how users describe the way the cult product makes their skin feel.
Clinique global brand president Michelle Freyre said the brand had seen an “outpouring” of consumers talking about Moisture Surge beyond its functional skincare benefits.

“With the ‘Feels Like Moisture Surge’ campaign, we are bringing consumer voices forward — in their own words — highlighting all the ways consumers describe Moisture Surge while staying deeply grounded in Clinique’s dermatologist-guided science,” Freyre said in a media release.
Jones, who is herself a Moisture Surge user, said her relationship with Clinique predates the campaign.
“I trust Clinique because I’ve grown up with it. I’m excited to be a part of the Clinique family and represent a brand whose products I genuinely love and trust,” she said.
The Moisture Surge range takes centre stage as Clinique turns real consumer conversations on Reddit into inspiration for its latest global campaign.

Closer to home, Clinique is building on the Moisture Surge franchise by pairing its Moisture Surge Active Glow Serum with the familiar 100H Auto-Replenishing Hydrator in what it calls the “Glow Chain Effect”.
The two-step routine combines gentle exfoliation, hydration and brightening, with the serum applied first followed by the gel-cream moisturiser.
The Active Glow Serum contains lactic acid to exfoliate dead surface skin cells, hyaluronic acid for hydration and Vitamin C to help brighten the appearance of skin.
Clinique said in-vitro testing found that its 100H Hydrator penetrated 2.1 times better when applied after the Active Glow Serum compared with using the moisturiser alone.
And Malaysians can now step into the Moisture Surge world themselves.
Clinique has transformed The Rabbit Hole in Kuala Lumpur into a pink-hued hydration destination from Sept 9 to Nov 9, bringing the campaign and its skincare story into a physical experience.
The takeover features product experiences, Instagram-friendly installations and a limited-time menu inspired by Moisture Surge.
3df096765311f0b9: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 13 — The remains of the five victims of the Flying Doctor Service (FDS) helicopter crash in Long Lellang, Baram, Sarawak, were handed over to their respective families this morning at the Forensic Department of Miri Hospital after their identities were confirmed through DNA analysis.

Health Minister Datuk Seri Dzulkefly Ahmad said the Ministry of Health (MOH) coordinated the transportation of the remains to their respective final resting places following official confirmation of their identities by the police and the Department of Chemistry.

He said the remains of medical officer Dr Ainul Baraah Kamarudin will be flown from Miri to Kota Bharu, Kelantan on a Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF) special aircraft before being buried at Seri Kedeper Muslim Cemetery, Kampung Baung, Pengkalan Chepa.

“The remains of nurse Debra Moset will be laid to rest at Kampung Semadang, Padawan tomorrow, while nurse Jessie Paya Jok’s remains will be taken to her home today, with her funeral to be held at BEM Cemetery Lambir, Miri tomorrow.

“The remains of assistant medical officer Alexson Adit Henry would be taken to his family home today, with the funeral scheduled for Tuesday (Sept 15) at Anglican Cemetery Lambir, Miri,” he said in a statement.

He said the remains of pilot Capt Zainol Afiq Bee Sham will be flown from Miri to Kuala Lumpur International Airport on a Malaysia Airlines flight before being buried at Forest Heights Muslim Cemetery, Senawang, Negeri Sembilan.
Dzulkefly expressed his appreciation to the Malaysian Armed Forces (MAF) for providing logistical support through the RMAF to facilitate the repatriation of the remains to Peninsular Malaysia.

He also thanked the police, Department of Chemistry, Fire and Rescue Department (JBPM), Sarawak Islamic Religious Department (JAIS), Miri Hospital management and all agencies involved, from the search and rescue (SAR) operation through to the handling of the remains.

Meanwhile, he said the ministry would continue to strengthen its strategic cooperation with JBPM to support the smooth implementation of medical evacuation (MEDEVAC) operations following the temporary suspension of FDS services to facilitate investigations, review and a comprehensive assessment.
He also expressed his appreciation to Malaysians for their concern, prayers and support for healthcare personnel and the victims’ families. — Bernama
919a8c573b161709: KULAI, Sept — Police fired one shot at the tyre of a car after a 23-year-old couple allegedly rammed a police motorcycle and tried to hit officers during an incident in Jalan Kenari, Bandar Putra, Kulai, early yesterday.

Kulai District Police Chief ACP Tan Seng Lee said the incident occurred at about 1.20 am when members of the district police headquarters’ Motorcycle Patrol Unit (URB) stopped a black Perodua Myvi in the area after finding it suspicious, with a local man and woman inside the vehicle.
“During the inspection, the suspects became aggressive and tried to flee by ramming the URB motorcycle and a public vehicle, a Mazda CX-5, besides attempting to hit the police officers.

“Following this, the URB personnel fired one shot at the tyre of the suspects’ vehicle to defend themselves and stop the vehicle. However, the suspects managed to escape,” he said in a statement today.
He said a URB officer suffered minor injuries to his leg after becoming trapped when the police motorcycle was struck by the suspects’ vehicle.
Tan said within 24 hours of the incident, Kulai police arrested the male and female suspects separately in Bandar Putra, Kulai and Kluang between 11.30 am and 8.30 pm yesterday.
Police also seized the black Perodua Myvi believed to have been used in the incident, along with a remote control.
Tan said preliminary urine screening tests on both suspects were negative, while checks found that neither had a previous criminal record.

“The motive for the incident is still under investigation. The case is being investigated under Section 307 of the Penal Code for attempted murder, Section 332 for voluntarily causing hurt to a public servant and Section 186 for obstructing a public servant in the discharge of his duties,” he said.
Both suspects will be brought before the Johor Bahru Magistrates’ Court today for a remand application. — Bernama
42f5a48c29bd5224: PETALING JAYA: The flash floods and landslides that occurred at several areas in Tanah Rata, Cameron Highlands, on Friday were not caused by the bypass road project, the public works department (JKR) said.
It said the project remains in the design and assessment study stage, and no physical construction has been carried out on-site, other than routine maintenance on existing roads.

It was responding to concerns raised regarding flash flood incidents and landslides following heavy rain at several locations in Cameron Highlands, including calls for the temporary suspension of the bypass road project.
The project involves the construction of the Tanah Rata bypass road, the upgrading of the federal road from Tanah Rata to Kea Farm, and the upgrading of another federal road, Jalan Griddle.

In a statement, the department said preliminary checks indicate that the flooding at the Mardi park and public field areas in Tanah Rata occurred on secondary roads, which are not part of the main road alignment involved in the project.
However, a small-scale landslide did occur at Jalan Tengkolok, an area falling under the scope of routine maintenance by the project contractor.
Debris clearing operations were carried out immediately and have been completed to ensure the safety and smooth flow of traffic for road users, it said.
"The works ministry takes seriously all concerns regarding slope safety, geological conditions, drainage systems, and disaster risks," it said.

"The implementation of this project is subject to all assessments, approvals, and technical conditions stipulated by the relevant authorities, including the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), Social Impact Assessment (SIA), geotechnical requirements, and local authority approvals.
"Physical construction work will only commence once all approvals and relevant approvals and conditions have been met."
d54841144f333541: KUANTAN: A trader lost RM315,963 after scammers posing as education office staff duped her into paying for 37 projectors in a bogus order.

Pahang acting police chief Datuk Azry Akmar Ayob said the 52-year-old victim, who runs a photocopying and printing shop, transferred the money to purchase the projectors before requesting the supplier's company registration documents.
He said the scam began on Sept 1 when the victim received a WhatsApp message from a man who introduced himself as Shahrizal and claimed to represent the Kuala Kangsar education office.
Shahrizal initially asked her to prepare a quotation for supplying examination papers before contacting her again on Sept 10.
"Shahrizal placed an order for two projectors to be sent to the Kuala Kangsar education office.
"As the victim's company did not have the projectors in stock, the suspect told her to contact an individual known as Jacky to arrange for the items.

"The victim ordered the projectors from Jacky and paid RM18,498. She later received an image purportedly showing that the two projectors had been delivered to the education office," he said in a statement today.
Azry said Shahrizal contacted the victim again on Sept 11 and informed her of another order for 50 projectors, providing a Local Order to convince her.
"The victim contacted Jacky and paid RM297,465 for the first batch of 35 projectors into a bank account belonging to PNCK Trading.
"After making the payment, the victim requested PNCK Trading to provide its company registration documents and tax identification number, but received no response.

8129babfeef03be5: JAKARTA: Indonesian rescuers were searching on Sunday for 140 people from a passenger ship that was earlier reported missing in the Java Sea after 103 others were evacuated, one of whom died, a search and rescue agency official said.

8c8f783083f08090: SINGAPORE, Sept 13 — Consumers looking for a new laptop or desktop may want to think twice, as PC prices here have skyrocketed by as much as 40 per cent amid a global shortage of key components.

The squeeze is being driven largely by the artificial intelligence boom, which is consuming huge quantities of computer memory, storage and graphics cards as companies expand data centres, The Straits Times reported today.

The average price of a regular laptop in Singapore rose 26 per cent year-on-year to S$1,650 (RM5,200) in the second quarter of 2026, from about S$1,300 (RM4,100), according to the latest data from research firm IDC.
Regular desktops were up 28 per cent to S$1,410 (RM4,450), while gaming desktops jumped 39 per cent to nearly S$1,860 (RM5,870). Gaming laptops rose 17 per cent to S$2,890 (RM9,110).
The biggest pressure point is RAM, or computer memory, as manufacturers divert production towards companies building AI infrastructure, where demand and profit margins are higher.

“Since last year, the PC market has seen significant price hikes, driven largely by the memory shortage crisis that has affected the whole information technology industry,” IDC Asia Pacific associate research analyst Ho Jin Wei was quoted as saying.

The Straits Times said it checked at Singapore’s Sim Lim Square and found the average price of a 32GB DDR5 RAM kit had nearly quadrupled from S$195 (RM615) in August 2025 to S$763 (RM2,410) in August this year.

The average price of a 1TB internal solid-state drive more than doubled from S$149 (RM470) to S$328 (RM1,035), while Nvidia’s 5060 series graphics cards rose 44 per cent from S$572 (RM1,805) to S$824 (RM2,600).
IDC expects PC prices to remain elevated throughout 2027, with only a slight easing likely in the second half of the year.

“With major graphics card makers reportedly planning further price increases for their respective product lines in the last six months of 2026, this could push PC prices up further,” Ho was quoted as saying.
He added that any meaningful easing in PC prices was more likely to come in 2028 and beyond.

The squeeze is already being felt by Singapore’s computer retailers, with four shops at Sim Lim Square telling The Straits Times that sales had fallen by between 20 per cent and 80 per cent this year compared with 2025.
John Soroya, owner of R Zech Laptop, said sales of new and refurbished computers had plunged 80 per cent.
“It’s very, very difficult. Sometimes we cannot cover our rent,” he said.
Some consumers are now holding off purchases in the hope that prices will fall, while businesses and enthusiasts continue buying despite the higher costs.
Bizgram sales assistant Bryan Fun said some customers had bought computers two to three months ago because they feared prices would rise further, but more were now taking a wait-and-see approach.
He said suppliers had also informed the store that motherboard prices rose by about 10 per cent in September.
1f3cf38f31bf5856: PETALING JAYA: Government spokesman Fahmi Fadzil has rejected claims by certain quarters that court action and enforcement agencies are being used to threaten Umno leaders.

20055d7ddabc0c8b: PETALING JAYA: Pegawai kadet Pasukan Latihan Pegawai Simpanan (Palapes) perlu melengkapkan diri dengan ilmu diperlukan kerana medan pertahanan semakin kompleks dan ancaman terhadap negara tidak lagi terhad kepada peperangan konvensional.

1733c0c56c00a788: NEW DELHI, Sept 13 — Brics leaders stated in a joint declaration on Saturday the need to strengthen energy security, ensure stability of energy markets and uninterrupted supply of energy resources.
“We recognise that energy security is a crucial foundation for social and economic development, national security and the welfare of all nation,” the declaration following the New Delhi summit read.
The declaration also emphasised the need for energy security through stable supplies and protection of infrastructure.

“We highlight the need to enhance energy security by ensuring energy market stability and maintaining undisrupted flows of energy from diverse sources, strengthening value chains, ensuring resilience and protection of critical energy infrastructure, including cross-border infrastructure,” the document said.
Brics leaders have also called for the creation of more reliable and stable supply chains that take into account the needs of developing countries, according to the New Delhi declaration.

It said that Brics leaders are concerned by ongoing conflicts in the world, as well as the polarisation and fragmentation of the world order, according to the leaders’ declaration of the association’s summit in New Delhi published on Saturday.
“We express concern about ongoing conflicts in many parts of the world and the current state of polarisation and fragmentation in the international order,” the declaration read.
Brics countries call on the international community to respond to challenges through diplomatic measures, according to the declaration.
The declaration further stated that Brics countries expressed concern over growing risks linked to the nuclear threat and conflict.
“We express concern about the growing risks of nuclear danger and conflict,” the document read.
Brics countries also emphasised the need to step up the disarmament and arms control system, according to the declaration.
Brics leaders also highlighted the deliberate attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities subject to IAEA safeguards, according to a declaration adopted at the group’s summit in New Delhi on Saturday.

“We express serious concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities under full safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), in violation of international law and relevant resolutions of the IAEA.
“Nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm,” the document read.
The 18th Brics summit is being held on September 12-13 in New Delhi. — Bernama-Sputnik/Ria Novosti

1248d3a2160191c6: VIENTIANE: Isolated, under-developed Laos brands itself the "Battery of Southeast Asia", powering its neighbours with dozens of hydroelectric plants, but frequent power outages leave its own people in the dark.
Exports of electricity to neighbouring countries including Thailand and Vietnam are a key source of revenue for the landlocked nation, designated as a least developed country by the UN.
But most of the power generated leaves the country and, combined with an ageing grid, that results in frequent outages and sometimes having to import electricity to meet demand.
When the power cuts out after dark in Vientiane, families wander outside to avoid the stifling heat indoors, using cell phones to light their way.
At one of the two main public hospitals, a doctor in the pediatrics emergency department is used to watching medical equipment suddenly shut down until the generators kick in.
"Over the past three to six months, we've often faced electricity problems, especially at the children's centre," said the doctor, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
"A ventilator came to a halt, but we do have a generator at the hospital."
When old wiring recently caused an electrical fire in the alley outside the hospital, a blackout cut power to X-ray, ultrasound and ventilator equipment, she said.
Elsewhere in the city, a front-desk staffer at a health clinic said power outages occurred two to three times a week, usually announced beforehand.

Without a generator, "we have to reconnect the electricity from a store next to us", said the staffer, who also requested anonymity in a one-party communist state where authorities do not tolerate dissent.
When the power is restored, the cry rings out across the city: "It's back!"
Direct lines
Laos exported around two-thirds of its total generated electricity in 2023, according to the World Bank, but experts say that figure is now even higher.
One former technical expert at state utility Electricite du Laos (EDL) put the figure at around 80%.
In the decade to 2024, annual electricity exports more than tripled, from 12 terawatt-hours (TWh) to 38 TWh, according to official data -- enough to power Paris for a year and a half.
In 2023, they brought in US$2.65 billion, according to the government, often sold in deals struck by the state with businesses that invest in Laos's infrastructure.
"Transmission lines from most projects are 'dedicated' to their customers," said Grant Hauber, an Asia adviser at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.
"Meaning they are not connected domestically to Laos consumers."

Much of Laos's distribution grid dates back to the 1970s, and now struggles to keep pace with an increasingly modern economy of tourism, massive infrastructure, urban development and air conditioning.
In Vientiane, a power line once used for one household now covers whole apartment blocks with many units, straining old transformers.
In rural areas, if a tree falls onto the power lines, it can cause a blackout for one village, sometimes several, because there is no backup.
Bounchan Manochit, a shop owner in northern Luang Prabang province, said that with no lights, wild animals may enter residents' homes at night.
"We can't see them," she said. "It can be dangerous."
Foreign investment
Almost all of Laos's population of eight million has access to electricity, up from just 15% in 1995, according to the government.
But EDL, charged with maintaining the grid, is tackling large debts incurred during the expansion and due to consumer subsidies.
With hydropower accounting for 80% of production as of 2024, supply dwindles in the dry season from March to August.
At times, Laos has struggled to provide power to its neighbours and finds itself importing energy, at significant cost, according to a recent World Bank report.
"Electricity production has already fallen short of domestic demand and export contracts on several occasions," it said.
Laos's main export market is Thailand but it is diversifying its client and energy mix.
Vietnam has recently stepped up imports, including through Laos's Monsoon Wind project, the region's largest wind farm that became operational last year.

Researcher Le Hong Hiep of the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute noted the growing demands of Vietnam's manufacturing sector and the country's own issues with energy production -- but said politics also played a part.
"Vietnam also wants to import more electricity from Laos to increase its leverage over Laos," part of a wider contest with China for influence in Vientiane, he said.
The energy from the Monsoon Wind project is destined only for Vietnam.
"Zero for local," noted the former expert at EDL.
6d602851e5c11c0b: HYDERABAD, Sept 13 — Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed that “differences should not become disputes” as they met on the sidelines of the Brics Summit in New Delhi on Saturday.
The two leaders welcomed the steady progress in India-China bilateral relations since their last meeting in Tianjin in August 2025, India’s External Affairs Ministry said in a statement.

“They reaffirmed that both countries should take a strategic and long term perspective of their ties. Differences should not become disputes,” it said, adding that Modi emphasised that India-China relations must be guided by “mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.”
Xi’s previous visit to India was in October 2019 for an informal summit with Modi in Mamallapuram, near Chennai.
However, relations became strained following a military clash in 2020 along the disputed border.
The two sides have since considerably improved their relations through talks involving senior military and political leaders, while trade has grown significantly in recent years.
The Indian Prime Minister emphasised that “peace and tranquility in the border areas remains an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations,” the ministry said.

“He underlined the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border related issues. The two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question, proceeding from the political perspective of their overall bilateral relations and the long-term interests of the two peoples,” it said.

The talks also covered efforts to enhance cultural exchanges and business linkages, while the two sides agreed to address each other’s concerns over trade imbalances, supply chain issues and market access.
India recorded a trade deficit of US$112.1 billion (RM456.6 billion) with China out of total bilateral trade of US$151.1 billion (RM615.7 billion) in 2025-26, according to government data.
China will assume the Brics chairmanship next year and host the 19th Brics Leaders’ Summit. — Bernama
02412056d62fd16c: NEW DELHI, Sept 13 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim may have been in New Delhi for high-level diplomacy but his rendition of Kishore Kumar’s classic Khwab Ho Tum Ya Koi Haqeeqat struck a different chord, drawing positive reactions from many Indians.

dc54d8854e6cdcf0: NEW DELHI, Sept 13 — Members of the 11-nation Brics group including China, Russia, Iran and India called for calm in the Middle East at a summit in New Delhi on Saturday, overcoming earlier divisions to issue a joint statement.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, who joined Russian, Iranian, Indian and other leaders in India’s capital, told the summit that the Middle East war “does not serve the common interests of the international community”.

Foreign ministers of the Brics grouping had failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.

But leaders issued a statement on Saturday after intense diplomatic efforts by host India, as the bloc seeks to bolster its global influence and address conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.

“We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia,” the joint statement said, adding the countries “call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation”.
Brics was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

“We have to transform this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership,” Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders as he opened the two-day summit.
Modi said Brics nations “represent 50 percent of the world’s population, 40 percent of global GDP and more than 25 percent of global trade”.
But finding balance in the bloc is a tough diplomatic task.
India maintains cordial relations with both Iran and US ally Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

Iran’s Pezeshkian attended the summit shortly after warning that the Middle East does not need the United States to be a “regional policeman”, with the two countries at war and tensions threatening the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Pezeshkian met with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the summit sidelines.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Modi embraced Putin before talks on Friday. The Russian president, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners.
‘Handling differences’
Xi’s participation is also being closely watched because it is his first visit to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honour guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.

“Although our two countries are different in many respects, they are fully capable of complementing each other’s strengths, supporting one another, achieving mutual success and advancing together,” Xi said as he met Modi, in a video released from New Delhi.

His visit comes six years after a deadly military clash along the disputed Tibetan border between China and India, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border.
India’s foreign ministry said in a statement after the meeting that “the two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question”.
Modi “underlined the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border related issues,” the foreign ministry added.
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry continuing to complicate ties.

“Both sides should... work hand-in-hand to promote high-quality major financial cooperation, advocate an equal and sustainable global order, and foster an economic globalisation that is open and inclusive,” Xi said.

Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday – exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 – waving placards against Xi’s visit. — AFP
5aee223366c7cb6a: PETALING JAYA: Sanusi Nor berkata sukar untuk PAS melakukan pelarasan dan peralihan kerusi dengan Umno jika perundingan tertumpu dalam konteks sesebuah negeri sahaja, merujuk Kedah, Kelantan, dan Terengganu.

Justeru, pengarah pilihan raya PAS itu, menyeru medan perbincangan diperluaskan melibatkan seluruh negara bagi membolehkan pelarasan kerusi dibuat antara negeri, termasuk kemungkinan pertukaran kawasan ditandingi.

“Saya sebut dulu di peringkat negeri Melaka, rundingan tak boleh dibuat peringkat negeri Melaka sahaja. Rundingan mesti ambil kira seluruh negara. Barulah boleh buat 'adjustment' (pelarasan) sana sini. 'Swapping' (penukaran) tak 'swapping', tak boleh 'swapping' dalam negeri, swapping negeri lain.

42c6fde8876aec58: SEPT 13 — There are some things you don’t realise you miss until you are far away from home.

When we travelled from Malaysia to China to work as educators, we expected the usual challenges that come with living abroad—adjusting to a new environment, learning new routines, navigating unfamiliar surroundings and, of course, adapting to a different food culture.
But nobody really prepares you for the small cravings.

The sudden longing for something you have eaten countless times without ever thinking twice about it. The kind of craving that makes you realise that food is not simply about hunger. Sometimes, it is about familiarity.

One day, a group of us started talking about poori. We were all Malaysian educators working in China, and somehow, we had collectively developed the same craving. That conversation could easily have ended with, “I miss Malaysian food.” Instead, I thought, Why not make it ourselves?

So I decided to make poori using my mother’s recipe. Poori is a popular South Asian deep-fried flatbread made from unleavened dough. It is typically rolled into small rounds and fried until it puffs up into a light, golden, crispy bread.
Perhaps this is what happens when you live far away from home. You begin to appreciate the things you once took for granted.
Recipes that once seemed ordinary suddenly become precious. The way your mother makes something, the taste you grew up with, even the little imperfections of a homemade meal begin to carry meaning.
I followed my mother’s recipe as best as I could, and for the accompaniment, I decided on sardine sambal.
It was not an elaborate meal.
There was no fancy plating or carefully curated menu. It was simply poori and sardine sambal, made in a Chinese kitchen by a Malaysian who was missing a taste of home.
Yet, when I served it to my colleagues, something interesting happened. Everyone ate. Within 10 minutes, everything was finished.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Making and eating 'pooris' in China... more than just a yearning for a familiar taste. — Pictures by Matthuri Palanee

That moment made me think about why food matters so much when we are away from home. We often talk about adapting to another country as though it is simply a matter of becoming comfortable with new surroundings.
But adapting does not necessarily mean leaving everything familiar behind. Sometimes, adapting means finding ways to carry a little bit of home with us. And food does exactly that.
A plate of poori can carry memories. A particular sambal can remind us of family. A familiar smell can transport us thousands of kilometres away without us ever leaving the room.
More importantly, food creates community. We were not just colleagues that day.
We were a group of Malaysians who shared the same craving, sitting together and enjoying something that reminded us of home. That simple moment united us.

Perhaps it was because we were all experiencing life away from Malaysia together. Perhaps it was because, for those few minutes, we were no longer thinking about work, responsibilities or the unfamiliarity of being in another country. We were simply enjoying something that belonged to all of us.

The poori became more than a meal. It became a shared experience—a small reminder that even when we are far from home, we are not necessarily alone. It also reminded me that homesickness does not always arrive dramatically.

Sometimes, it arrives quietly. It appears when you suddenly crave your favourite breakfast. When you miss the food your mother used to make. When you realise that the meal you never thought twice about back home is something you now have to make yourself.
And perhaps that is not necessarily a bad thing. Being away from home has taught me to value home differently.
Malaysia is no longer just the country I came from. It is in the recipes I remember, the flavours I recreate, the food I share and the memories I carry with me.
That day in China, I did not bring Malaysia back with me. I simply brought a plate of poori to the table. But for 10 very happy minutes, it felt like home had come along too.
Maybe that is the real power of food. It does not need to travel with us in our suitcases. It travels in our memories, in our hands and in the recipes passed down to us.

And sometimes, when we find ourselves thousands of kilometres from home, all it takes is a little flour, a mother’s recipe, some sardine sambal and a group of hungry Malaysians to remind us where we came from — and to remind us that even far from home, a simple meal can bring people together and make strangers feel a little more like family.

9305597ecbcb732c: SANTIAGO: More than 280 people were arrested in Chile during demonstrations commemorating victims of Augusto Pinochet's military dictatorship, the government said Saturday.
This year was the first since the end of Pinochet's brutal 1973-1990 rule that Chile did not hold any official events marking the era that left deep scars on the South American nation.

"I cannot erase history, nor can I ask our compatriots to accept that we are condemned by our history to be unable to look toward our nation's future," said president Jose Antonio Kast, the first far-right head of state in Chile since Pinochet's exit, who took office in March.
Under Pinochet more than 3,200 people were killed or disappeared, while tens of thousands of others were tortured or imprisoned.
Demonstrations take place annually to mark the Sept 11, 1973 coup d'etat led by Pinochet against the government of socialist president Salvador Allende.
This week's protests saw demonstrators throw sticks and stones at riot police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons.
Authorities arrested 284 people on Thursday and Friday, public security minister Martin Arrau said on X, noting it was an 80% increase from the previous year.
Those arrested included 16 foreign nationals and 31 minors, Arrau said.
There were 198 "incidents of violence" but no civilian injuries, he added.
The biggest demonstration took place at Santiago's General Cemetery, home to the Allende family mausoleum, with leftist former president Gabriel Boric joining the rally.
Other events took place at the presidential La Moneda Palace, where Allende died by suicide, and at the National Stadium, which the Pinochet regime used as a site for detention and torture.

b77d3fb0db102a4e: SEOUL: South Korea’s main stock exchange is extending into evening sessions, breaking with Asia’s trading-hour norms to tap what it hopes will be sustained demand from global investors.

In a step toward its goal of 24-hour trading, Korea Exchange will on Monday enable trading through 8pm for nearly all local stocks, following the regular close at 3.30 pm. Though the first of its kind among major Asian exchanges, the move tracks a global trend toward around-the-clock markets, led by Nasdaq Inc and New York Stock Exchange.

After the stock market’s world-beating run this year on AI enthusiasm, Korea Exchange aims to capture broader international participation, particularly during European business hours. Monday’s rollout will offer a test of the bourse’s ability to sustain sufficient liquidity through a longer day and prove that investors actually want the extra time even as interest in Korean equities cools.

“The longer trading window generally means more flexibility for investors, and that makes the market more efficient,” said Young Jae Lee, senior investment manager at Pictet Asset Management in London. “Investors who are more trading-oriented with higher turnover, or hedge fund types may use it more frequently.”

After-hours trading isn’t entirely new in Korea. Alternative trading system Nextrade introduced pre-market and evening sessions in March 2025, covering about 600 stocks, and grabbed nearly a third of activity within a few months of its launch.

Korea Exchange’s latest move takes it a step further, opening about 2,400 Kospi and Kosdaq stocks for evening trades, including short-selling. Exchange-traded funds are excluded for now. The bourse also plans to launch pre-market hours by the end of 2027.
This is “another step in the ongoing evolution of Korea’s capital markets and their accessibility to global investors,” said Edward Kim, head of Korea equities sales at Bank of America.

Few expect an immediate uptick in activity when the new hours open. Whether it can draw sufficient volume remains a key question, especially given the thin liquidity seen after the currency-market extended hours in July.

The Kospi index more than doubled this year through its peak amid an AI frenzy, before a sudden souring of sentiment led to a 22% selloff in July and a sharp contraction in turnover. The benchmark remains up 64% for 2026, still the world’s best-performing major gauge.

Foreign funds will wait and see if there are actually enough buyers and sellers in big stocks like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix during the evening hours before risking big trades there, said Dave Mazza, chief executive officer of Roundhill Financial.
“Extending the hours does not create liquidity; it redistributes it,” Mazza said, adding that initial interest is likely to be modest.

Nextrade’s experience may be an indication. Its data show retail investors made up more than 80% of its non-regular trading, while erratic price swings and the lack of institutional participation also posed challenges.

How big investors can hedge currency effectively is another issue. Korea’s foreign exchange market technically runs 24 hours, but off-peak trading can be thin, which may make hedging more costly and discourage foreign funds from committing large capital to evening stock trading.

Liquidity may also affect prices. Moving a large block of shares in the evening risks paying far more or selling for less than expected in a thin market, said Sanghyun Park, founder of Clepsydra Capital.
“The biggest risk is just getting caught in low liquidity,” Park said.

Despite lingering issues, market watchers broadly back the extension as it gives investors a quicker way to react to late-breaking news or earnings. The recent listing of SK Hynix’s American depositary receipts was another sign of Korea opening up to foreign investors, but served as a limited channel for mainly chip stock exposure.

“The after-market session promotes market equality by enabling a wider range of investors to react to post-close news, thereby reducing information asymmetry, and enhancing overall market fairness,” said Tony Cheung, execution consultant specialist at Instinet.

e54ac31fcea530c7: I have been working in higher education institutions for more than three decades. In those 30 years in the United Kingdom and Malaysia, I have not seen such a difficult environment for higher education.

In the United Kingdom the Office for Students has forecast that around 43% of these institutions are likely to report deficits in 2025–26. Of the 119 providers, 24 are potentially at risk of exiting within 12 months.

Some are already merging. Kent and Greenwich universities have launched the London and South East University Group starting this year and King’s College London and Cranfield University have plans for 2027.

In the United States analysis by EY-Parthenon identified 442 vulnerable private nonprofit colleges and universities and about 26% of more than 1,700 institutions could close or merge within 10 years. More than 120 were placed in the highest-risk group, collectively serving around 670,000 students.

In Japan demand for university places could fall to 460,000 by 2040, only 73% of current capacity. More than 40% of private universities are reportedly operating at a deficit, with regional institutions most at risk.

In global markets many institutions depend heavily on international students. The problem is that visa restrictions, geopolitical tensions, falling domestic enrolment and heavy debt have quickly destabilised this model.

In Malaysia my research with the Penang Institute highlighted these risks a decade ago. There are currently around 1.3 million students in public and private higher education institutions. International enrolment is around 160,000, or 12.3%.

This looks strong but data from the higher education ministry shows that the number of private institutions fell nearly 15% from 436 in 2019 to 371 in 2025. This decline reflects mergers, change in status and registration adjustments, not just closures.

The main causes are demographics, costs and gig-economy opportunities but artificial intelligence (AI) will accelerate the crisis as students increasingly reject expensive programmes built around generic learning models and assignments in favour of cheaper, flexible learning not built on knowledge delivery alone.

In this very competitive market, it is trusted brands that will survive, as well as institutions with strong finances or donors, distinctive programmes, industry partnerships, personalised learning, flexible credentials and lifelong learning.
The new Triple Alliance between Sunway University, Monash University Malaysia and Taylors in the education hub in Bandar Sunway aims to address these challenges.

The logic is that by pooling academic, technological and infrastructural resources the three universities can build strong foundations for themselves and strengthen Malaysia’s position as a regional talent and innovation hub.
Resource pooling, combining student and staff numbers allows the three universities to explore joint research grants, share facilities and build new cross-institutional programmes.
It can also break down internal silos and exchange entrepreneurial and management best practices. Eventually they can launch joint multi-disciplinary initiatives leveraging each other’s strengths.

It aligns with Malaysia’s development goals to target “high-value”, finance-generating sectors in AI and digital, health and sustainable technologies. This fits in well with the recently-launched Malaysia Higher Education Blueprint 2026–2035.
It also builds scale to attract regional talent and industry partnerships and generate sustainable revenue and cost efficiency.
As such this alliance has real benefits but it will also consolidate market share and prestige in these elite member institutions.
This poses a real challenge to smaller private universities who must create smart alliances, mergers and takeovers to survive. I said this 10 years ago — but who listens to me?

3a9078f2a9629205: If we sit long enough at a neighbourhood mamak restaurant or walk through a housing area during a festive open house, we will almost certainly see a version of Malaysia that warms the heart.

We will see an unspoken, everyday grace — neighbours helping neighbours without checking identity cards, youths playing football across cultural lines, and ordinary people sharing a quiet, unbothered pluralism.
It is the unglamorous bedrock of national survival, the messy, beautiful space where we actually live — the middle ground.
Yet running parallel to this is a very different reality: political machineries and machinations designed to dismantle this exact peace.
Human beings are wonderfully complicated. We carry within us a crowded pantheon of loyalties—we are neighbours, workers, parents, children of a specific soil, and participants in a shared civic life.
But our race- and religion-based political systems have a perennial, lazy habit of trying to strip away all that overlapping complexity and force us down into a single, unyielding box.
Decades ago, the Lebanese-French essayist Amin Maalouf warned that humanity was perpetually trapped in a tribal reflex that reduced a person to a single, belligerent affiliation.
When identity is treated like a fortress rather than a bridge, politics stops being an art of negotiation and becomes an exercise in keeping people out.

The philosopher Amartya Sen called this the “miniaturisation” of human beings—the deliberate political push to shove individuals into a preordained tribal category while erasing everything else that they are.
We can watch this ancient script play out in real time in contemporary Malaysia, particularly through the majoritarian identity strategies championed by several parties.
The latest iteration of this was seen at the PAS muktamar on Sept 5, where a motion was passed to strengthen Malay Muslim political unity ahead of the next general election.

On paper, the rhetoric often sounds noble, coated in religious obligation and duty. And to be clear, there is nothing morally wrong or criminal in calling for Muslim unity — indeed, many in PAS and elsewhere frame it as a spiritual and communal duty.
Yet there is a profound historical irony. Islamic political ethics and classical scholarship have long warned against ‘asabiyyah’ — tribal fanaticism and blind group chauvinism.

Most of us know that political actors have a habit of masking their appeals in the universal language of faith and unity while weaponising group feeling to draw an invisible, suffocating circle around the nation.

To make a singular identity pitch work, political architects must manufacture a profound sense of paranoia. They must convince the group that they are under constant, existential threat, painting a picture of a civilisation right on the brink.

For instance, we have heard politicians from several parties — PAS, Umno, Bersatu, and even former prime minister Mahathir Mohamad — openly claim that Islam is under threat in Malaysia or that Malays are losing their land, their Tanah Melayu.
This manufactured fear crowds out rational, ethical concern — economic well-being, clean governance, and cross-cultural empathy — replacing it with the adrenaline of tribal survival.
The immediate casualty of this game is that fragile middle ground I mentioned above.

Exclusive identity politics — whether involving Malays, Chinese, Indians, Kadazandusuns or Muslims and non-Muslims — leaves zero room for moderation. Anyone who steps outside the tribal line or tries to build a bridge across communities may be branded a traitor to the cause.

It herds citizens into a zero-sum game, demanding that they view their neighbours — the very people who helped them shovel mud during floods or shared office space with them for years — not as fellow human beings, but as demographic adversaries.

Unity for an exclusive group always requires an “out-group” to define itself against. Calling for Muslim unity means drawing a circle to leave out the non-Muslims, just as calling for non-Muslim unity will draw a circle to leave out the Muslims.
Inside these invisible boundaries drawn by political players are those who fit the preferred mould; outside are millions of Malaysians who are instantly relegated to permanent political outsiders.

The long-term cost of this is deeply corrosive. A country cannot split its soul down demographic or religious lines without hollowing out its institutional backbone. When every ordinary civic issue is dragged into the tribal mud, compromise becomes impossible, and the state begins to fracture from within.

Malaysia sits today at a profound crossroads. On one side is the exhausting, vital work of defending the middle ground — the everyday commitment to a plural society where differences are respected rather than weaponised. On the other lies the comfortable, seductive trap of the single affiliation, where politicians harvest short-term wins by promising supremacy to one group at the expense of everyone else.

True political maturity takes the courage to step away from the politics of paranoia, protect our fragile middle ground, and heed the timeless warning: that a house built on the exclusion and subjugation of its own people can never truly stand.

As we celebrate the formation of Malaysia, we need to move away from the politics of identity to what I would call the politics of citizenship — where we are all citizens regardless of our racial origin or religion, and where Malaysian unity trumps all other unities.

5715c82c84cf543f: Last week, US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent launched an “economic D-Day” programme, intended to cut Iran off from all trading partners. So far, this intensified economic blockade has only contributed to an escalation of the US-Iran war, rather than moving it towards a conclusion.
That probably will not change, because China is unwilling to cooperate. And this is the reality that US policymakers must now face: Most possible paths to lasting peace run through China.

Wars end because one side gives up, or because influential people on both sides grow tired of the losses and want to move on, or because a powerful third party imposes peace. Seen through this lens, the US-Iran conflict could last for a long time.

Hardliners on both sides are now deeply entrenched. Iran is not about to surrender, the US will not risk a full-scale invasion, and China, the only third party with enough clout to make a difference, seems inclined just to watch. Bessent’s economic isolation campaign is unlikely to prove decisive without the support of Iran’s most important trading partner.

If China continues to do business with Iran, the current Iranian leadership will most likely survive. Any US threats against China remain non-credible, given China’s leverage over the supply of critical minerals needed by the sectors driving economic growth in the US and other major countries. No critical minerals means no computer chips—and no AI-led investment boom for the US.
Iran and the US agreed to a ceasefire in June, and this was quickly followed by a memorandum of understanding (MoU). But none of this has led to real peace.

Iran is still effectively limiting passage through the Strait of Hormuz, and the US is still turning away most vessels associated with Iran. The MoU looked good on paper, but it was never fully implemented by either side.

When the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, and Iran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz, some strategic thinkers believed that China would press for a quick resolution of the conflict, primarily because, until recently, as much as 60% of its oil imports passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
But this turned out to be a miscalculation. China had more than 1.2 billion barrels—200 million above its usual reserves—when the conflict began, and still holds more than 1.15 billion barrels today.
At the same time, the disruption and increase in global oil prices have accelerated demand for renewables and electric vehicles, which has helped China’s exports.
Ironically, these sectors are the same ones in which China has huge excess capacity. In that sense, the current crisis has postponed the financial losses in these sectors.

Overall, China turned out to be one of the least sensitive countries to the current crisis. This should be an important consideration in any future calculations by US policymakers and rules out instability in the Middle East as part of the toolkit for containing China.
The main loser from this war is the broader Middle East. The world economy is learning how to survive with oil and gas exports from the region at around half of their prewar level.

Of course, it is a relatively costly adjustment, but the longer this crisis continues, the less sensitive the world economy may become to disruptions in the Middle East. This may not be good news for the region’s oil-exporting countries, and they are likely to lose market share over the medium term.
Countries in the region, especially Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar, have also learned that reliance on US security may not work as well as they thought.

Saudi Arabia is trying to increase its reliance on other regional allies, while Qatar and the UAE are talking directly with Iran and using economic incentives to buy some security for themselves. These shifts support the argument that regional economic integration must be part of the solution to the current impasse.
At first glance, more diplomacy by regional players may strengthen the case for the US washing its hands of the issue and leaving the problem to Iran’s neighbours.

But it is very hard to see how the nuclear issue would be addressed in this scenario, and without addressing that concern about Iran, it may be very hard to make any long-term plans or even achieve partial economic integration in the region.

The only stable solution to this crisis is one that involves China and increases economic integration in the region, as well as addressing the nuclear issue by integrating Iran’s programme into a regional civilian electricity production supply chain led by China.

Chinese president Xi Jinping is due to visit Washington at the end of September. Perhaps the US-Iran conflict can be resolved in the context of a broader discussion with President Donald Trump. Or perhaps China will be content to watch and wait.

9f228d8d08f8675c: Nvidia spent a whopping $20 billion late last year to license Groq’s AI accelerator tech and hire away key members of its engineering team in an everything-but-the-kitchen-sink deal. The acquihire technically left Groq’s core inference-as-a-service business intact, but was clearly architected in such a way as to fly under regulators' radar. Only it didn’t. This week, The New York Times reported that the US Department of Justice had launched an antitrust probe into the deal. It’s hard to argue that Nvidia didn’t strip the startup for parts. It may not have been a merger in the traditional sense, but without its engineering staff, Groq may as well be Nvidia’s puppet at this point. Despite this, Nvidia contends the deal is a great American success story. “The Groq story is a prime example of the American system working as designed to promote innovation, reward entrepreneurs, and benefit consumers. The law is designed to encourage America's startup ecosystem and promote the fundamental rights of inventors and workers to pursue their dreams,” an Nvidia statement provided to El Reg and other media reads. Whether the acquihire of Groq actually harmed competition is another matter entirely. But, even if the Justice Department did force Nvidia to unwind the team, it’s probably too late. What exactly did Nvidia buy? Nvidia’s Groq acquihire bought it two key assets: mature silicon and the talent necessary to continue its development. Groq – which, by the way, is completely unrelated to Elon Musk’s Grok model series – made a name for itself using SRAM-heavy dataflow accelerators to speed up LLM inference to hundreds and now thousands of tokens a second, something that GPU-based systems from Nvidia had struggled to do on their own. But while faster than GPUs, the accelerators couldn’t achieve rapid throughput. Think of it this way: If Groq’s LPUs were the F1 cars, Nvidia’s GPUs were more like a city bus. But combine the two and you get something more akin to a sport pickup. At GTC in March, Nvidia unveiled its LPX racks, which are powered by 256 Groq-3 accelerators. As we understand it, they are really lightly modified versions of the startup’s existing Groq-2 chip designs, which makes sense, because three months is absurdly fast to tape out new silicon. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang promised Groq-3 combined with its Vera Rubin GPU racks would deliver optimal performance across the entire spectrum of inference workloads. But, as we’ve discussed at length now, disaggregated compute architectures are not unique to Groq. Nvidia rival Cerebras is building similar systems with AWS and AMD, SambaNova is working with Intel, and d-Matrix and its partners are combining its in-memory compute platform with Nvidia GPUs to the same end as Nvidia’s Vera Rubin-LPX rack combo. The damage, if any, has been done Deals of this sort that are engineered to avoid regulatory scrutiny should get it anyway, several US senators have argued. While Nvidia didn’t outright buy Groq on paper, it may as well have. However, the real question for the DOJ is whether the deal was harmful to competition, and given the competitive landscape, proving harm may be easier said than done. But even if the DOJ found reason to litigate and was successful in unwinding the deal — it certainly wouldn’t be the first time regulators had torpedoed an Nvidia deal — it probably wouldn’t change much. Before Nvidia and Groq announced their licensing deal, the GPU giant was already laying the foundations for an ecosystem with its networking business at its center. In late 2024, the company contributed its MGX rack designs to the Open Compute Project (OCP) making it possible for any chipmaker to put their chips in racks originally designed for Nvidia GPUs. Then in mid-2025, GPUzilla opened its high-speed interconnect tech — the secret sauce that makes six dozen GPUs behave as one — to the broader industry through a licensing scheme called NVLink Fusion. As we recently discussed, the combination of open racks and Nvidia networking effectively meant that any chipmaker licensing the tech could slot their designs directly into Nvidia’s racks. If the DOJ blocked the acquihire and unwound the deal, Nvidia might lose direct control of LPU development and any revenues from the sale of the chips, but it wouldn’t necessarily be the end of its Groq LPX racks. Groq would just join the growing number of Nvidia hardware partners designing around the company’s AI factory ecosystem. In fact, if anything, the acquihire ensures that even if regulators eventually derail the deal, there will be plenty of alternatives lined up and ready to fill the void. ®
